candidate_concepts.label: Problem Framing Definition
candidate_concepts.description: Problem framing is the process of discovering, analyzing, and defining the real strategic problem before committing to solutions.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain what problem framing means in their own words.
Student can distinguish problem framing from problem solving.

candidate_concepts.label: Problem Framing vs Problem Solving
candidate_concepts.description: Problem framing identifies the right question to ask, while problem solving finds the answer.
coverage_criteria: Student can articulate the difference between framing and solving with an example.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article states 'Problem framing is different from problem-solving because it is about discovering the right question to ask, while problem-solving is about finding the right answer.' in the FAQs.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This distinction is a key teachable point that can be assessed with a simple compare-and-contrast question.

candidate_concepts.label: Premature Convergence
candidate_concepts.description: Premature convergence is the brain's tendency to seek closure quickly under uncertainty, leading to locking onto the first plausible explanation or solution.
coverage_criteria: Student can define premature convergence and give an example.
Student can identify a scenario where premature convergence occurs.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article describes premature convergence in the neuroscience section and cites research.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This cognitive bias is a specific mechanism that can be checked with definition and scenario questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Pattern Completion Bias
candidate_concepts.description: Pattern completion pushes our brains to fill gaps with familiar narratives, even when the problem is new.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain pattern completion and how it leads to jumping to solutions.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article lists pattern completion as one of the three mechanisms driving premature convergence.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a distinct cognitive bias that can be assessed independently.

candidate_concepts.label: Confirmation Bias
candidate_concepts.description: Confirmation bias leads people to seek evidence that supports their initial interpretation rather than challenging it.
coverage_criteria: Student can define confirmation bias and relate it to premature convergence.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article mentions confirmation bias as a mechanism of premature convergence.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: It's a well-known bias but taught here in the context of problem framing, making it a relevant checkable concept.

candidate_concepts.label: Organizational Pressures to Jump to Solutions
candidate_concepts.description: Organizational systems like business case templates, status meetings, and budgeting processes push teams toward quick solutions before problem understanding.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least two organizational practices that reinforce solution-jumping.
Student can explain how these practices hinder problem framing.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article dedicates a section to organizational dynamics that reinforce solution-jumping.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept encompasses multiple examples integrated into a single teachable point about organizational culture.

candidate_concepts.label: Double Diamond Model for Problem Framing
candidate_concepts.description: The Double Diamond model consists of Discover (diverge) and Define (converge) phases for identifying and framing a problem before developing solutions.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the two phases of the first diamond.
Student can explain why these phases are important for problem framing.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article presents the Double Diamond model as a structured approach to problem framing.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a core framework that can be assessed by asking the student to recall and apply it.

candidate_concepts.label: Problem Reframing Technique
candidate_concepts.description: Problem reframing involves restating a strategic question to uncover different solutions, risks, and opportunities, as shown in examples like asking 'Which customer problems would drive sustainable growth?' instead of 'How do we grow revenue 20%?'
coverage_criteria: Student can give an example of reframing a problem.
Student can explain how reframing led to a better outcome in one of the provided examples.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article provides multiple examples of problem reframing with before-and-after scenarios.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is teachable by asking the student to apply reframing to a new situation.

candidate_concepts.label: AI Amplifies Bad Framing
candidate_concepts.description: AI tools optimize around the problem framing they are given, so poorly framed problems lead AI to efficiently solve the wrong problem, often failing to deliver business value.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why bad framing leads to AI project failure.
Student can describe an example from the article where AI didn't improve outcomes due to framing.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explicitly states 'AI tools are only as good as the questions they are given' and provides an example with customer service AI.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept ties problem framing to modern AI challenges, making it relevant and checkable with a scenario.

candidate_concepts.label: Building a Problem Framing Culture
candidate_concepts.description: Leaders can instill a culture of problem framing by shifting focus from 'how to fix' to 'why is this happening', establishing habits like asking reflective questions, standardizing problem statements, and adding a diagnostic phase.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least three habits or rituals that encourage problem framing.
Student can explain why these habits help prevent solution-jumping.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article's section 'Building a Culture That Stays in the Problem Space' provides specific practices.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept packages multiple actionable habits into a single teachable idea about cultural change.

candidate_concepts.label: Problem Framing Enables Execution Clarity
candidate_concepts.description: A well-framed problem clarifies ownership, metrics, and cross-functional involvement, leading to better execution with fewer mid-course corrections.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how clarity from problem framing impacts execution.
Student can identify what aspects of execution are clarified (ownership, metrics, teams).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The section 'From Framing to Ownership and Execution' explains this link.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a direct outcome of good framing, teachable with a cause-effect question.
